lesson.title: Moving Without Cost: The Logic of Passive Transport
lesson.summary: Passive transport lets substances cross the selectively permeable membrane without any expenditure of cellular energy, simply by following the same physical tendency that drives molecules from crowded regions toward less crowded ones.
lesson.body:
The selective permeability of the plasma membrane, covered in the previous chapter, determines which substances can cross and by what route. Passive transport describes movement that happens without the cell spending any of its own energy, in the form of ATP, to make it happen. Instead, passive transport relies entirely on a concentration gradient, meaning a difference in the concentration of a substance between one side of the membrane and the other, and on the physical tendency of molecules to spread from where they are more concentrated toward where they are less concentrated.

This tendency is not some special property of living cells. It reflects a basic physical principle related to entropy, the tendency of any system to move toward its most probable, most spread-out arrangement. Molecules are always in constant, random motion due to their thermal energy, and simple statistics means that random motion, applied to a crowd of molecules, produces net movement away from a crowded region and toward emptier space, purely by chance, until the concentration evens out. A cell does not need to spend energy directing this; it happens on its own as long as the membrane allows the molecule through.

Passive transport takes two main forms depending on the substance involved. Simple diffusion, covered in detail in the next chapter, is the direct movement of small nonpolar molecules straight through the phospholipid bilayer, following the selective permeability rules established earlier. Facilitated diffusion covers substances that cannot cross the hydrophobic bilayer unassisted, larger polar molecules and ions, but that still move down their concentration gradient with the help of a channel or carrier protein. The key point is that facilitated diffusion is still passive: the transport protein does not push the molecule against its gradient or consume ATP to move it. It only provides a path through the membrane that would otherwise be blocked.

It helps to see what passive transport is not. Active transport, a related process built on this same foundation but not covered in depth in this chapter, moves substances against their concentration gradient, from low concentration toward high concentration, and that direction of movement always requires an input of cellular energy because it works against the natural spreading tendency of molecules rather than with it. Passive transport, by definition, only ever moves substances in the direction they would already tend to go on their own.

A cell relies heavily on passive transport for ordinary maintenance because it is metabolically cheap: no ATP is spent moving oxygen into a cell or carbon dioxide out, since both diffuse down their existing gradients as long as the gradient exists in the right direction. Maintaining that gradient in the first place, though, often does require active work elsewhere in the cell, a distinction worth keeping in mind. The next two chapters look closely at the two central examples of passive transport in biology: diffusion in general, and osmosis, the specific diffusion of water.
